headline: Big 5 Construct Saudi Closes After Four Days in Riyadh
deck: More than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries, five co-located shows, three Impact Trail awards and a programme dominated by localisation and operations.
excerpt: Big 5 Construct Saudi closed on 2 September after four days at Riyadh Front, having drawn more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources. Impact Trail awards went to PRIMECO, Masdar and Al-Futtaim Engineering.
content:
Big 5 Construct Saudi closed on 2 September after four days at the Riyadh Front Exhibition & Conference Center, having brought more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries into a single venue at ROSHN Front alongside King Khalid International Airport.

The show ran under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources and was opened by Eng Fawaz bin Badr Al Shora, Deputy Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources for Industrial Services and Compliance. The organiser's stated expectation ahead of the event was more than 35,000 trade visitors across the four days, which ran from 4pm to 10pm daily. Its theme was framed around building from foundation to future, at every scale.

The event is structured as five shows in one venue. The main Big 5 Construct Saudi halls covered general construction and building materials, with Heavy Saudi Arabia taking heavy equipment onto an outdoor site of more than 20,000 square metres with live demonstrations, Totally Concrete Saudi Arabia covering concrete production and materials, HVACR Saudi Arabia covering cooling, ventilation and refrigeration, and Saudi FM & Clean covering facilities management, cleaning and waste.

Three awards were made under the Big 5 Impact Trail, the show's sustainability programme. Prime Middle East Trading Company, which trades as PRIMECO, won sustainability innovation for its work with Honeywell's Solstice low-global-warming-potential refrigerant solutions. Masdar won best circular economy solution for its Kronospan carbon-negative wood-based panels and engineered boards. Al-Futtaim Engineering Company won operational sustainability for an integrated facilities management solution. The Impact Trail also spotlighted work from Galaxy Technology, exhibiting Albion Valves with carbon transparency across its cast-iron range, Star Factory in spray polyurethane foam roofing and waterproofing, and Keller in ground improvement and foundation engineering.

The conference programme ran alongside the exhibition across nine topic areas: codes, standards and regulations; health and safety; sustainability; artificial intelligence; technology; project management; concrete; modular construction; and HVACR. Sessions addressed navigating the Saudi Building Code, improving concrete quality, strengthening project governance, applying artificial intelligence in project delivery, and improving coordination between HVACR design, installation and facilities management.

Speakers came from across the Saudi delivery chain. Organisations represented on the programme included the Saudi Building Code Center, ROSHN Group, SEVEN, Misk City, Saudi Binladin Group, Kabbani Construction Group, Al Kholi Group, Modern Building Leaders and Dussman Ajlan & Bros. Christopher Seymour, managing director for the Middle East and Africa at Mace Consult, and Shonagh Kinnaird, project director at Misk City, both spoke on sessions examining collaboration between stakeholders, digital transparency, procurement and lessons from Saudi Arabia's major developments.

The commercial backdrop is a construction market still expanding. Saudi Arabia's contracting register has passed 140,000 firms, project awards have rotated towards infrastructure, and the giga-project programme continues to generate demand across materials, equipment and services. The organiser says the previous edition of the show generated more than $1bn in business engagements, a promoter's figure that describes intent rather than contracted value.

What distinguished this edition was less the scale than the composition of the questions being asked in the halls. Localisation dominated: manufacturers wanted Saudi partners, Saudi distributors and, in a growing number of categories, Saudi production. That has a regulatory driver behind it, with the Local Content and Government Procurement Authority requiring minimum local content percentages on a widening list of products for public procurement. Facilities management and operations occupied more commercial attention than they have at previous editions, as assets built over the past decade reach handover. And technology on the floor moved decisively towards things that can be measured: robots doing defined tasks, sensors reporting from inside structures, and equipment sold with published performance data rather than claims.

The show returns to Riyadh next year. Its co-located sections will be measured against a Saudi construction programme that is still awarding work at scale but is increasingly judged on delivery rather than announcement.
